what: where a page load spends its instructions once the compile is gone - the residual the image cannot delete
metric: INSTRUCTIONS (callgrind Ir), not wall clock. A share here is not a share of time - a cache miss costs one instruction and hundreds of cycles - so this says where the WORK is, and page-load.json says what it costs.
page: p5-basic.html: an inline flag, the 4.5 MB p5 bundle and a sketch, all three handed over as images
how_this_was_measured: ctpageload BUILDS the images it hands over, so profiling the whole run measures the compile it exists to avoid - which is how the first callgrind run in this project was wasted. The image arm is therefore a named, noinline function and callgrind is told to collect only inside it: valgrind --tool=callgrind --collect-atstart=no '--toggle-collect=*ctpageload_load_from_images*'

586,350,095 instructions collected, against a whole-process count that is dominated by the compile. The tool asserts that no script was compiled from source on that path, so a run that fell back would not be recorded as this.
findings: THE BASELINE'S OWN DESCRIPTION OF THIS RESIDUAL IS WRONG, and that is the most useful thing here. page-load.json says what remains is 'HTML parsing, CSS, style, layout and the image load itself'. Measured: HTML parsing is 0.0%, CSS and style together are 0.5%, and layout, paint and raster do not appear at all. Those four are under one percent of the work between them.

WHAT ACTUALLY REMAINS IS TWO THINGS. The IMAGE LOADER is 26% - the single largest item, and bigger than anything it replaced on this path. And RUNNING p5's OWN TOP LEVEL is most of the rest: interpreter 17.4%, property and object access 12.0%, allocator 8.2%, regex 6.4% - about 44% together, which is a 4.5 MB library building its API surface, not the engine's page pipeline.

SO PHASE 16A AND 16B WOULD BUY ALMOST NOTHING ON THIS PAGE. A compiled DOM blueprint and a compiled style program target the 0.5% that HTML, CSS and style cost here. That is a real answer to a real question - the ordering in the master plan assumes they matter - and it is measured rather than argued. It says nothing about a page that is mostly markup; it says a great deal about the corpus this project is justified by.

AND THE LOADER IS NOW THE THING TO OPTIMISE, which it was not before. Its operand pass alone - the check_slot lambda - is 7.49% of everything on this path, which is fifteen times what the whole CSS engine costs. The bound-table rewrite already took 19.74 ms to 19.18; this says where the rest of it is.

THE INTERPRETER'S SHARE IS NOT THE 1.4% THIS PROJECT QUOTES, and the two numbers are not in conflict. docs/performance.md measures a page load that INCLUDES compiling 4.5 MB of JavaScript, where the compile drowns everything; this measures the same page with the compile removed, in instructions rather than time. Once an image deletes the parse, what is left is a fifth interpreter by instruction count. Neither figure licenses a claim about what an AOT backend would save in milliseconds - that needs its own measurement, and page-load.json's 19 ms is the ceiling it would be a fraction of.
